title: A second way into the same routine
desc: Give a routine extra entry points — schedule, webhook, app event — without copying it, and test each one separately.
learningGoal: After this lesson you can add an extra entry point to a routine, tell which trigger kinds may be added beside the primary one and which replace it, and start a dry-run from the entry point you want to test.

steps.title: One routine, three front doors
steps.bodyMd:
Van Dijk Groep, a 40-person installation firm, has an invoice-intake routine. It starts on an app event: a new e-mail with an attachment in the invoices mailbox.

Now two more ways in are wanted. Their accounting portal should be able to push an invoice straight in, and at 07:00 the routine should sweep up anything that arrived overnight.

The tempting answer is to duplicate the routine twice. Three copies means three places to fix a mistake, and within a month they will have drifted apart.

A routine can instead carry **more than one entry point** — the same steps, several ways to start them. That is what this lesson is about.

steps.title: One primary trigger, plus extras
steps.bodyMd:
The canvas is blunt about it: **"Every routine has exactly one trigger."** That one is the **primary** trigger. It can be any of the seven kinds, and it can never be deleted — right-click it and Delete is refused with "The primary trigger cannot be removed".

Beside it, a routine may carry **additional triggers**. Only three kinds qualify:

- **On a schedule** — run at a fixed time, over and over
- **On webhook call** — run when an HTTP request arrives
- **On app event** — run when something happens in a connected app

**Trigger manually**, **On form submission**, **When an agent calls it** and **From a Studio App** can only ever be the one primary trigger.

steps.title: Which way in, and may it be an extra?
steps.instruction: Van Dijk Groep listed five ways people might want to start the invoice routine. Match each one to the entry point it needs — and notice which of them can only be the primary trigger.

pairs.left: The accounting portal should push each approved invoice straight in over HTTPS.
pairs.right: On webhook call — may be added as an extra
pairs.note: A webhook is one of the three kinds allowed beside the primary trigger.

pairs.left: At 07:00 the routine should pick up anything that arrived overnight.
pairs.right: On a schedule — may be added as an extra
pairs.note: Schedules became addable as extra entry points alongside webhooks and app events.

pairs.left: A new e-mail with an attachment lands in the invoices mailbox.
pairs.right: On app event — may be added as an extra
pairs.note: This is Van Dijk's current primary trigger, but the kind is also allowed as an extra.

pairs.left: Small suppliers without a portal should upload an invoice on a public page.
pairs.note: A form trigger publishes a hosted page for the routine; it can only be the one primary trigger.

pairs.left: The office manager wants to ask an assistant in chat to run it for one supplier.
pairs.right: When an agent calls it — primary only
pairs.note: An agent trigger exposes the routine as a tool in chat, and only as the primary trigger.

steps.question: Van Dijk's routine already runs on the Gmail app event. In the Editor, someone opens the Trigger menu on the add-step ribbon and picks "On form submission", hoping suppliers can use a public page as well. What happens?

choices.label: A dialog asks "Replace the App event trigger with Form?" — confirm and the Gmail trigger, with its settings, is gone.
The form trigger is added beside the Gmail trigger, giving the routine two ways in.
choices.feedback: Only schedule, webhook and app event can sit beside a primary trigger. In the menu, those three read "Adds another way to start this routine"; the other four read "Replaces the current trigger".

choices.label: The Trigger menu does not list Form at all once a routine already has a trigger.
choices.feedback: All seven kinds stay listed and searchable — hiding them left people unable to change a routine's trigger at all. What changes is the description under each one, and whether picking it asks first.

choices.label: It is added as an extra trigger, and you then set its Trigger kind to Form in the inspector.
choices.feedback: On an extra trigger the Trigger kind list offers only Schedule, Webhook and App event. There is no route to Form there — a value that is not allowed shows as "(unsupported here)" and is disabled.

steps.explanation: The confirmation says it plainly: "A routine can only have one trigger of these kinds, so the current one and its settings are replaced." The button reads Replace. If Van Dijk wants a supplier form as well, the form needs its own routine — with the shared work in a reusable Step both routines call.

steps.title: Adding an extra entry point
steps.bodyMd:
Open the routine, stay in the **Editor** view, and use the **Trigger** menu on the add-step ribbon — or type "webhook" into **Search a step…**, which returns triggers too.

Every item tells you which sort it is:

- **Adds another way to start this routine** — schedule, webhook, app event
- **Replaces the current trigger** — the other four

A replacing pick always asks before it does anything, because a search result should never quietly throw away someone's trigger.

One scope rule: the Trigger menu is not offered inside a flowlet or a reusable Step. Extra entry points belong to the routine itself, not to a sub-flow.

steps.title: A new trigger arrives unconnected
steps.bodyMd:
The new trigger lands on the canvas as a second starting point with **no line out of it**. Nothing is wired for you.

That matters, because a run only walks the steps it can reach from the trigger that actually fired. A new trigger with nothing connected will fire happily and the run will end having done nothing at all.

So draw a connection from it into the step that should run first. A step may take a line from both triggers — whichever one fires, it runs once, from that side.

What each entry point hands over differs: a webhook's posted body is not the same shape as an app event's message. Steps that read from the trigger need to cope with both, or each entry point needs its own first step.

steps.title: Put Van Dijk's webhook in place
steps.instruction: The accounting portal needs to push invoices into the existing routine. Put the six moves in the order that gets there without a broken call in production.

items.label: Open the invoice routine and switch to the Editor view
In the ribbon's Trigger menu pick "On webhook call" — it reads "Adds another way to start this routine"
Draw a connection from the new Webhook node to the step that should run first
Set Start from to the new Webhook trigger and choose Dry-run (preview)
Press Activate so the routine accepts inbound calls
Copy the trigger’s URL from its Endpoint panel and hand it to the portal team

sim.feedback: Wire before you test: an unconnected trigger dry-runs to nothing and looks fine. Test before you activate: a dry-run takes no real action, so a mistake costs nothing. And hand out the URL last — a call to a paused or draft routine is refused with "Automation is not active".

steps.title: Testing one entry point at a time
steps.bodyMd:
The run control in the builder header is a split button. The visible half is **Dry-run** ("Dry-run — no real actions, a safe preview"); the chevron beside it ("More ways to run") opens **Dry-run (preview)** and **Run live**.

Once a routine has more than one entry point, that menu grows a **Start from** group listing the primary trigger and every additional one by name. Pick the entry point first, then Dry-run or Run live starts the walk there.

Without it you would only ever be testing the primary path, which is exactly the half that already worked. For app-event triggers, **Diagnose** in the header probes the pipeline behind them: subscription, credentials, filter.

steps.title: Your turn: plan Van Dijk's second entry point
steps.instruction: Van Dijk Groep's invoice routine runs on the Gmail app event. Write a short plan (4–6 sentences) for giving it the 07:00 overnight sweep as a second way in. Name the trigger kind you add and say why it is allowed beside the primary one, say what the new trigger connects to and what happens if you forget that, and describe how you would test it before anything goes live.
steps.placeholder: e.g. I add an On a schedule trigger, because schedule is one of the three kinds allowed as an extra entry point beside the Gmail app event, which stays the primary trigger. On the canvas it arrives unconnected, so I draw a line from it to …

steps.title: Four ways this goes quiet
steps.bodyMd:
**Nothing is wired from it.** The trigger fires, the run finishes, no step ran. The run history shows it as finished — this is the one that fools people.

**The routine is paused or still a draft.** A webhook call is refused with "Automation is not active"; a form page only works when the routine is active and not a draft. There is one activation for the whole routine, not one per entry point.

**An app-event trigger with no provider or event.** Validation refuses it — the trigger "has no provider/event — it can never fire" — and activation is blocked until you pick both.

**A schedule with no valid pattern.** An extra schedule is held to the same rules as the primary one, so it cannot sit active with no next run.

An extra trigger you no longer want deletes like any other node; only the primary one refuses, with "The primary trigger cannot be removed".

steps.question: Van Dijk added a webhook as a second entry point, wired it into the first step and saved. The portal team reports that every call comes back refused with "Automation is not active". What is wrong?

choices.label: The routine is paused or still a draft — press Activate in the builder header.
The portal is signing the request wrongly, or replaying an old value in the nonce header.
choices.feedback: Both of those are real failures, but they are refusals about the caller's credentials, not about the routine. This message names the routine's own state.

choices.label: The invoice payload is over the 256 kB limit the webhook accepts.
choices.feedback: The 256 kB body limit is real, but an oversized body is refused for its size. The message here says the routine is not active, which is a different thing entirely.

choices.label: Extra triggers have their own switch, and only the primary trigger was activated.
choices.feedback: There is one activation per routine — the Pause/Activate control in the header — and it covers every entry point. There is no per-trigger switch to miss.

steps.explanation: Activation is the gate for everything inbound: a webhook only accepts calls, and a form page only serves, when the routine is active and no longer a draft. Activate also runs the strict validation pass, so it is where an incomplete extra trigger is caught.

steps.title: Add a second way in
steps.instruction: Open one of your own routines in the Editor view. From the ribbon's Trigger menu add "On a schedule" or "On webhook call" — the ones that read "Adds another way to start this routine" — then draw a connection from the new trigger into the step that should run first. Finish by picking it under Start from and taking a dry-run.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.bodyMd:
- **Add an entry point instead of a copy.** Schedule, webhook and app event can sit beside a routine's primary trigger; manual, form, agent call and Studio App replace it, and the dialog that asks you to confirm is your last warning.
- **Connect what you add.** A new trigger arrives with no line out of it, and a run only walks what it can reach from the trigger that fired.
- **Test each door on its own.** Start from in the run menu lets you dry-run from one entry point at a time, and activation is what finally opens the inbound ones.

ex-routine-extra-triggers-plan.title: Plan a second entry point
ex-routine-extra-triggers-plan.task: Plan an extra entry point for a routine that already runs on a Gmail app event: which kind is added and why it is allowed, what it connects to and the cost of forgetting, and how it is tested before going live.
criteria: Names an entry point that is genuinely allowed as an extra — a schedule (or a webhook or app event) — and says the existing Gmail trigger stays as the primary one.
States that the new trigger arrives unconnected and must be wired into the step that should run first, because a run only walks what it can reach from the trigger that fired.
Describes testing it before it counts: picking the new trigger under Start from and taking a dry-run rather than a live run.
Mentions that activation is what makes the routine usable, or that a dry-run takes no real action.
ex-routine-extra-triggers-plan.guidance: Do not pass an answer that adds a form, manual, agent-call or Studio App trigger as an extra entry point — those replace the primary trigger. Do not pass an answer that assumes the new trigger automatically runs the existing steps, or that treats a live run as the way to test it. An answer that only names the trigger kind, with nothing about wiring or testing, is below the bar.

practiceTopic.title: Extra entry points on a routine
practiceTopic.summary: How a routine gains more than one way to start, which trigger kinds may be added beside the primary one, and how each entry point is tested.
facts: Only three trigger kinds can be added as extra entry points: On a schedule, On webhook call and On app event.
Trigger manually, On form submission, When an agent calls it and From a Studio App can only ever be a routine's one primary trigger.
In the ribbon's Trigger menu an addable kind reads "Adds another way to start this routine" and the rest read "Replaces the current trigger".
Picking a replacing kind asks first: "A routine can only have one trigger of these kinds, so the current one and its settings are replaced."
On an extra trigger the Trigger kind list offers only Schedule, Webhook and App event; a value that is not allowed shows as "(unsupported here)" and is disabled.
The run menu grows a Start from group once a routine has more than one entry point, listing the primary trigger and every additional one so a run can be started from the one you want to test.
A run only walks the steps reachable from the trigger that fired, so a new trigger with no connection out of it does nothing.
A webhook call to a paused or draft routine is refused with "Automation is not active"; extra triggers are not offered inside a flowlet or a reusable Step.

actionChecks.label: Give a routine a second entry point
actionChecks.hint: In Studio, Automations: open a routine in the Editor, add On a schedule or On webhook call from the ribbon's Trigger menu, and wire it into a step.

endpoints.returns: { automations: [...] } — the caller's own routines, each with id, title, isDraft, isActive and its definition

criteria.label: A routine of your own exists
criteria.hint: Create one from the Automations start screen, or open an existing one. The extra trigger is stored inside the routine’s definition, where this check cannot look — the second trigger card on the canvas is your proof.
criteria.rule: GET /api/automation/ → automations[] is non-empty (definition.triggers is per row and not readable by the runtime)
